lead: A WDM network carries many lightpaths, each on a wavelength. Its nodes must add, drop and cross-connect those wavelengths without turning every signal into electronics. An optical add-drop multiplexer handles a few local wavelengths; an optical cross-connect switches many wavelengths between many fibers. A lightpath normally keeps one wavelength from end to end, the wavelength continuity constraint, and converters are used only where that fails. Routing and wavelength assignment choose the path and the wavelength. These ideas run metro rings, data-centre links and long-haul mesh networks.
prereq: You need: lightpaths, links and protection (Optical network concepts) and the circulator and Bragg grating (Passive devices).

sections.h3: Nodes that add, drop and cross-connect

blocks.text: An optical node does more than join fibers. It adds local wavelengths, drops wavelengths for local receivers, and passes the rest through. An optical add-drop multiplexer (OADM) does this for a few wavelengths. A fixed OADM drops chosen wavelengths with gratings and circulators or thin-film filters. A reconfigurable OADM (ROADM) uses a wavelength-selective switch (WSS), which sends each wavelength from its input to any chosen output port. The WSS changes the route of a wavelength, not the wavelength itself.

An optical cross-connect (OXC) switches many wavelengths between many input and output fibers, so it can rearrange lightpaths across a mesh. A metro ring uses OADMs to drop one wavelength at a city exchange while the others pass untouched; a long-haul mesh node uses an OXC.

Size first. Take an OXC with F fiber pairs and W wavelengths per fiber. Each input fiber is demultiplexed into its W wavelengths. Without wavelength converters, wavelength λ<sub>i</sub> can only leave on λ<sub>i</sub>, so the node is W separate F × F switches, one per wavelength plane: W × F² crosspoints in crossbar form. With full wavelength interchange, any of the F × W inputs can reach any of the F × W outputs, which needs one (FW) × (FW) switch: (FW)² crosspoints, plus converters.

In broadcast-and-select, each input fiber is split into as many copies as there are output fibers. At each output, a filter and a gate on each copy keep the wanted wavelength from that input and block the rest, and a combiner sums the copies. Loss is the splitter loss plus filter and gate loss plus the combiner loss, and a closed gate that still leaks a little sets the crosstalk. A WSS-based node routes each wavelength instead of sending all power everywhere, so its loss and crosstalk are lower, at higher cost.

blocks.text: Millisecond elements suit circuit switching of lightpaths; nanosecond elements are needed for burst and packet switching.
A lightpath keeps one wavelength from source to destination unless a converter changes it. For a path with links 1 to k, let S<sub>i</sub> be the set of free wavelengths on link i.

blocks.where: S<sub>i</sub> is the set of free wavelengths on link i; k is the number of links; S is the set of wavelengths free on every link. Without conversion the path can be set up only if S is not empty.

blocks.text: Checking only neighbouring pairs of links is wrong: every link must share the wavelength. Converters relax the rule. Optoelectronic (O-E-O) conversion receives the signal, regenerates it and retransmits it on a new wavelength. Cross-gain modulation in an SOA (Optical amplifiers) lets a strong signal at λ1 modulate the gain seen by a probe at λ2, copying the data onto λ2. Four-wave mixing (Nonlinear effects covers the Kerr effect behind it) creates a copy at a new wavelength in a nonlinear medium. Converters are placed sparsely, because each adds cost, loss and noise.

Routing and wavelength assignment (RWA) picks a path and a wavelength for each lightpath. In route-first-then-assign, find a route (for example the shortest path by Dijkstra), list the wavelengths free on all its links, and take the lowest-numbered one (first fit). If none is free, try the next route or block the request. Static traffic is known in advance and can be planned; dynamic traffic comes and goes, so the blocking probability matters. Static RWA is a graph colouring: each lightpath is a vertex, two vertices are joined when their paths share a link, and colours are wavelengths.

Protection reuses the ring ideas of SONET/SDH (UPSR and BLSR) and the mesh schemes 1+1 and shared backup paths; an OXC speeds restoration by switching whole wavelengths. Optical burst switching (OBS) sends a control packet ahead on a separate wavelength and the data burst after an offset time, so each node can set its switch before the burst arrives; contention can drop a burst. Optical packet switching (OPS) switches every packet, so it needs nanosecond switching, fast header processing and optical buffering.

examples.question: A lightpath must run A–B–C–D. Link A–B has λ1 and λ2 free, B–C has λ2 and λ3 free, and C–D has λ1 and λ3 free. (a) Can it be set up with wavelength continuity? (b) Node B has a wavelength converter. Find a working assignment. (c) A node has 4 fiber pairs with 8 wavelengths each. How many crosspoints does it need without converters, and with full wavelength interchange?
steps: Free sets: S<sub>AB</sub> = {λ1, λ2}, S<sub>BC</sub> = {λ2, λ3}, S<sub>CD</sub> = {λ1, λ3}.
(a) {λ1, λ2} ∩ {λ2, λ3} = {λ2}; then {λ2} ∩ {λ1, λ3} = ∅. No wavelength is free on all three links, so the request is blocked without conversion, even though every link has two free wavelengths.

(b) The converter at B splits the path into A–B and B–C–D. On A–B use λ2 (free). For B–C–D intersect {λ2, λ3} ∩ {λ1, λ3} = {λ3}, so use λ3 on both links. At B convert λ2 → λ3. One conversion is enough.
(c) Without converters: 8 wavelength planes, each a 4 × 4 switch with 4² = 16 crosspoints, so 8 × 16 = 128 crosspoints.
With full interchange: 4 × 8 = 32 inputs and 32 outputs in one 32 × 32 switch, 32² = 1024 crosspoints, plus up to 32 converters.
Check: 1024 ÷ 128 = 8 = W. Freedom to change wavelength costs W times more crosspoints.
examples.answer: (a) Blocked: the free sets have no common wavelength. (b) λ2 on A–B, convert to λ3 at B, λ3 on B–C and C–D. (c) 128 crosspoints without converters; 1024 with full wavelength interchange.

traps: A common wavelength on each pair of neighbouring links is not enough. The same wavelength must be free on every link of the path.
A WSS switches a wavelength to another port; it does not change it. Only a wavelength converter turns λ2 into λ3.
Without converters an OXC is W small F × F switches (W × F² crosspoints), not one big FW × FW switch. For 4 fibers and 8 wavelengths that is 128, not 1024.
Splitter losses in dB add: a 1:16 splitter costs 10 log₁₀ 16 = 12.04 dB, and a 16:1 combiner costs another 12.04 dB.
OADM and OXC are not the same: an OADM adds and drops a few local wavelengths on one fiber line, while an OXC can switch any wavelength between many fibers.

quiz.q: State the job of an OADM.
quiz.a: An OADM adds local wavelengths into a fiber, drops chosen wavelengths to local receivers, and passes the other wavelengths through unchanged.

quiz.q: In OBS, what is the offset time?
quiz.a: The gap between sending the control packet and sending the data burst, so the nodes on the path can set their switches before the burst arrives.

quiz.q: Why is a WSS called wavelength-selective, and what does it not do?
quiz.a: It routes each wavelength separately from its input to a chosen output, so it selects by wavelength. It does not convert a wavelength to a different value.

quiz.q: Why does OPS need faster switching than OBS?
quiz.a: OPS switches every packet, and a packet lasts nanoseconds to microseconds. OBS switches once per burst, which is much longer, and the offset time gives nodes time to set up.

quiz.q: Link A–B has λ1 and λ3 free; link B–C has λ2 and λ3 free. Can a lightpath A–B–C run without a converter? On which wavelength?
quiz.a: {λ1, λ3} ∩ {λ2, λ3} = {λ3}. Yes, on λ3 on both links.

quiz.q: A node has 6 fiber pairs and 16 wavelengths per pair. Find the crosspoints without converters and with full wavelength interchange.
quiz.a: Without converters: 16 planes of 6 × 6 = 36 crosspoints, so 16 × 36 = 576. Full interchange: 6 × 16 = 96 ports, 96² = 9216 crosspoints.

quiz.q: A broadcast-and-select OXC has 16 output fibers, so each input is split 1:16 and each output combines 16 copies. Estimate the loss and explain why amplifiers are needed.
quiz.a: Splitter 10 log₁₀ 16 = 12.04 dB and combiner 12.04 dB, so 24.08 dB before the filter and gate losses. A signal arriving at −10 dBm would leave below −34 dBm, so an EDFA or SOA is needed to restore the level.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one cost of placing a wavelength converter at every node.
quiz.a: Advantage: the continuity constraint disappears, so blocking falls and wavelengths are reused freely. Cost: each converter adds cost, loss, power use and noise, and the switch grows from W × F² to (FW)² crosspoints, so sparse placement is usually chosen.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern metro and data-centre networks use colourless, directionless ROADMs with WSS fabrics and flexible-grid optics, where the channel width itself can change. Software-defined control puts RWA and restoration in a central controller, and large data centres use optical circuit switches between racks. Search for elastic optical network, ROADM architecture and routing and spectrum assignment.
